claim: Dengue virus (DV) is a compact, icosahedrally symmetric, enveloped particle.
source: Dengue virus (DV) is a compact, icosahedrally symmetric, enveloped particle, covered by 90 dimers of envelope protein (E), which mediates viral attachment and membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dengue virus structure.

claim: Dengue virus is covered by 90 dimers of envelope protein (E).
source: Dengue virus (DV) is a compact, icosahedrally symmetric, enveloped particle, covered by 90 dimers of envelope protein (E), which mediates viral attachment and membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dengue virus structure.

claim: Envelope protein (E) mediates viral attachment and membrane fusion.
source: Dengue virus (DV) is a compact, icosahedrally symmetric, enveloped particle, covered by 90 dimers of envelope protein (E), which mediates viral attachment and membrane fusion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the E protein.

claim: Fusion requires a dimer-to-trimer transition of envelope protein (E).
source: Fusion requires a dimer-to-trimer transition and membrane engagement of hydrophobic 'fusion loops'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus fusion mechanism.

claim: Fusion requires membrane engagement of hydrophobic 'fusion loops'.
source: Fusion requires a dimer-to-trimer transition and membrane engagement of hydrophobic 'fusion loops'.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus fusion mechanism.

claim: Trimerization and membrane engagement are rate-limiting steps in West Nile virus membrane fusion.
source: We previously characterized the steps in membrane fusion for the related West Nile virus (WNV), using recombinant, WNV virus-like particles (VLPs) for single-particle experiments (Chao et al., 2014). Trimerization and membrane engagement are rate-limiting; fusion requires at least two adjacent trimers; availability of competent monomers within the contact zone between virus and target membrane creates a trimerization bottleneck.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chao et al., 2014).

claim: West Nile virus fusion requires at least two adjacent trimers.
source: We previously characterized the steps in membrane fusion for the related West Nile virus (WNV), using recombinant, WNV virus-like particles (VLPs) for single-particle experiments (Chao et al., 2014). Trimerization and membrane engagement are rate-limiting; fusion requires at least two adjacent trimers; availability of competent monomers within the contact zone between virus and target membrane creates a trimerization bottleneck.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chao et al., 2014).

claim: Availability of competent monomers within the contact zone between virus and target membrane creates a trimerization bottleneck.
source: We previously characterized the steps in membrane fusion for the related West Nile virus (WNV), using recombinant, WNV virus-like particles (VLPs) for single-particle experiments (Chao et al., 2014). Trimerization and membrane engagement are rate-limiting; fusion requires at least two adjacent trimers; availability of competent monomers within the contact zone between virus and target membrane creates a trimerization bottleneck.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Chao et al., 2014).

claim: Dengue VLPs from all four serotypes have an essentially similar fusion mechanism to West Nile virus.
source: We now report an extension of that work to dengue VLPs, from all four serotypes, finding an essentially similar mechanism.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small-molecule inhibitors of dengue virus infection that target E block its fusion-inducing conformational change.
source: Small-molecule inhibitors of dengue virus infection that target E block its fusion-inducing conformational change.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript showing inhibition of fusion.

claim: Approximately 12-14 bound inhibitor molecules per particle completely prevent fusion.
source: We show that ~12–14 bound molecules per particle (~20–25% occupancy) completely prevent fusion, consistent with the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Approximately 20-25% occupancy of inhibitor molecules per particle completely prevents fusion.
source: We show that ~12–14 bound molecules per particle (~20–25% occupancy) completely prevent fusion, consistent with the proposed mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Flaviviruses include dengue, tick-borne encephalitis, West Nile, and Zika viruses.
source: Flaviviruses, a family that includes dengue, tick-borne encephalitis, West Nile, and Zika viruses, are a group of mosquito-borne pathogens of substantial interest for vaccine and small molecule therapeutic development (Diamond and Pierson, 2015; Heinz and Stiasny, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Flaviviruses are mosquito-borne pathogens of substantial interest for vaccine and small molecule therapeutic development.
source: Flaviviruses, a family that includes dengue, tick-borne encephalitis, West Nile, and Zika viruses, are a group of mosquito-borne pathogens of substantial interest for vaccine and small molecule therapeutic development (Diamond and Pierson, 2015; Heinz and Stiasny, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diamond and Pierson, 2015 and Heinz and Stiasny, 2012.

claim: The envelope glycoprotein (E) is the membrane fusogen required for cell entry and infection.
source: The envelope glycoprotein (E) is the membrane fusogen required for cell entry and infection (Harrison, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harrison, 2015.

claim: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI), domain II (DII), and domain III (DIII).
source: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the subunit; domain II (DII: an extension emanating from DI) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip; domain III (DIII), with an immunoglobulin-like fold, connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin (Rey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Rey et al., 1995.

claim: Domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the E subunit.
source: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the subunit; domain II (DII: an extension emanating from DI) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip; domain III (DIII), with an immunoglobulin-like fold, connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin (Rey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Rey et al., 1995.

claim: Domain II (DII) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip.
source: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the subunit; domain II (DII: an extension emanating from DI) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip; domain III (DIII), with an immunoglobulin-like fold, connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin (Rey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Rey et al., 1995.

claim: Domain III (DIII) has an immunoglobulin-like fold.
source: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the subunit; domain II (DII: an extension emanating from DI) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip; domain III (DIII), with an immunoglobulin-like fold, connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin (Rey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Rey et al., 1995.

claim: Domain III (DIII) connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin.
source: E comprises three beta-sheet rich domains: domain I (DI) is a central beta barrel that organizes the rest of the subunit; domain II (DII: an extension emanating from DI) bears a hydrophobic fusion loop at its distal tip; domain III (DIII), with an immunoglobulin-like fold, connects to the C-terminal 'stem' and transmembrane helical hairpin (Rey et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citation to Rey et al., 1995.

claim: Flavivirus E proteins undergo conserved, fusion-inducing conformational rearrangements when exposed to reduced pH, from a pre-fusion dimer to a post-fusion trimer.
source: The conserved, fusion-inducing conformational rearrangements these proteins undergo when exposed to reduced pH, from a pre-fusion dimer to a post-fusion trimer, offer an opportunity to exploit the common structural features of all flavivirus E proteins to find viral entry inhibitors (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus fusion mechanism.

claim: The conserved conformational rearrangements of flavivirus E proteins offer an opportunity to exploit common structural features to find viral entry inhibitors.
source: The conserved, fusion-inducing conformational rearrangements these proteins undergo when exposed to reduced pH, from a pre-fusion dimer to a post-fusion trimer, offer an opportunity to exploit the common structural features of all flavivirus E proteins to find viral entry inhibitors (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the conserved nature of the fusion mechanism.

claim: A molecule of β-octyl glucoside (β-OG) was present in a pocket between DI and DII in a crystal structure of the dengue serotype 2 E dimer.
source: In a crystal structure of the dengue serotype 2 E dimer, a molecule of β-octyl glucoside (β-OG), used in the preparation, was present in a pocket between DI and DII (Modis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Modis et al., 2003.

claim: The pocket between DI and DII closes up during the fusogenic conformational change.
source: This pocket closes up during the fusogenic conformational change (Modis et al., 2004), and the observation that a small molecule can bind there suggested that it might be a good target for an entry inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Modis et al., 2004.

claim: The observation that a small molecule can bind in the pocket between DI and DII suggested that it might be a good target for an entry inhibitor.
source: This pocket closes up during the fusogenic conformational change (Modis et al., 2004), and the observation that a small molecule can bind there suggested that it might be a good target for an entry inhibitor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation that the pocket closes during fusion.

claim: A screen designed to detect small molecules that interfere with a step in the conformational transition yielded a series of cyanohydrazone compounds that bind a soluble DI-DII fragment.
source: Indeed, a screen originally designed to detect small molecules that interfere with another step in the conformational transition yielded a series of cyanohydrazone compounds that bind a soluble DI-DII fragment (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: Cyanohydrazone compounds block fusion in vitro and infection in cell culture.
source: These compounds block fusion in vitro and infection in cell culture; they bind the E protein on the virion surface before the virus attaches to a cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012 in the previous sentence.

claim: Cyanohydrazone compounds bind the E protein on the virion surface before the virus attaches to a cell.
source: These compounds block fusion in vitro and infection in cell culture; they bind the E protein on the virion surface before the virus attaches to a cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012 in the previous sentence.

claim: The most potent cyanohydrazone compounds inhibit viral infectivity with IC90 values in the single-digit micromolar range.
source: The most potent of them inhibit viral infectivity with IC90 values in the single-digit micromolar range (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: The β-OG pocket is the binding site for cyanohydrazones and several chemically distinct series of inhibitors.
source: Recent studies of the effects of mutation on members of several chemically distinct series of inhibitors, including the cyanohydrazones, confirm that the β-OG pocket is indeed their binding site (de Wispelaere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Wispelaere et al., 2018.

claim: Single-particle fusion measurements with WNV VLPs outlined steps in the transition leading to membrane merger.
source: In previous work on the mechanism of membrane fusion by West Nile virus (WNV) E, we used single-particle fusion measurements with WNV virus-like particle (VLPs) to outline steps in the transition leading to membrane merger (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chao et al., 2014.

claim: Trimerization of E into an extended intermediate becomes a kinetic bottleneck in progression to hemifusion.
source: We could interpret the observed, pH-dependent kinetics with a model in which trimerization of E into an extended intermediate, with the three fusion loops inserted into the target membrane, becomes a kinetic bottleneck in progression to hemifusion, because hemifusion requires collapse to the postfusion conformation of at least two adjacent trimers in a ~30 monomer contact zone between a virus particle and the membrane with which it is fusing (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from previous work (Chao et al., 2014).

claim: Hemifusion requires collapse to the postfusion conformation of at least two adjacent trimers in a ~30 monomer contact zone between a virus particle and the membrane with which it is fusing.
source: We could interpret the observed, pH-dependent kinetics with a model in which trimerization of E into an extended intermediate, with the three fusion loops inserted into the target membrane, becomes a kinetic bottleneck in progression to hemifusion, because hemifusion requires collapse to the postfusion conformation of at least two adjacent trimers in a ~30 monomer contact zone between a virus particle and the membrane with which it is fusing (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data from previous work (Chao et al., 2014).

claim: VLPs for the four DV serotypes were prepared by expression in 293 T cells at 28°C.
source: VLPs for the four DV serotypes were prepared by expression in 293 T cells, essentially as described for WNV VLPs (Chao et al., 2014). Expression was at 28°C rather than 37°C, as the latter yielded particles with substantially lower fusion activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Expression at 37°C yielded particles with substantially lower fusion activity than expression at 28°C.
source: Expression was at 28°C rather than 37°C, as the latter yielded particles with substantially lower fusion activity.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: DV4 VLPs have an inflection pH of 6.1 for bulk hemifusion.
source: We measured the pH dependence of bulk hemifusion and found sharply sigmoidal curves with inflection pH of 6.1 for the DV4 VLPs and ~5.4 for those of DV1, DV2 and DV3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: DV1, DV2 and DV3 VLPs have an inflection pH of approximately 5.4 for bulk hemifusion.
source: We measured the pH dependence of bulk hemifusion and found sharply sigmoidal curves with inflection pH of 6.1 for the DV4 VLPs and ~5.4 for those of DV1, DV2 and DV3 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy was used to determine single-particle dwell time distributions for hemifusion at pH 5.5.
source: We used total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy as described previously (Chao et al., 2014; Floyd et al., 2008; Ivanovic et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017) to determine single-particle dwell time distributions for hemifusion at pH 5.5 (Figure 2B), with dequenching of DiD-labeled VLPs to mark the moment of hemifusion with the supported lipid bilayer.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, supported by citations.

claim: Dequenching of DiD-labeled VLPs marks the moment of hemifusion with the supported lipid bilayer.
source: We used total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy as described previously (Chao et al., 2014; Floyd et al., 2008; Ivanovic et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017) to determine single-particle dwell time distributions for hemifusion at pH 5.5 (Figure 2B), with dequenching of DiD-labeled VLPs to mark the moment of hemifusion with the supported lipid bilayer.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: A pseudo-receptor was incorporated into the target bilayer to uncouple membrane attachment from exposure of the fusion loop triggered by the pH drop.
source: We incorporated into the target bilayer a pseudo-receptor, to uncouple membrane attachment from exposure of the fusion loop triggered by the pH drop.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The receptor was either the lectin domain of DC-SIGN-R linked through a histidine tag to a NiNTA-headgroup lipid or a similarly linked Fab from antibody 1AID-2, specific for DV2 domain II.
source: The receptor was either the lectin domain of DC-SIGN-R linked through a histidine tag to a NiNTA-headgroup lipid or a similarly linked, antigen-binding fragment (Fab) from antibody 1AID-2, specific for DV2 domain II (Chao et al., 2014; Lok et al., 2008; Tassaneetrithep et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the experimental materials used, supported by citations.

claim: There was no receptor-dependence of hemifusion dwell times.
source: We found no receptor-dependence of hemifusion dwell times; the data shown are with the DC-SIGN-R.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The dwell-time distributions show some differences among the four serotypes.
source: The dwell-time distributions in Figure 2B show some differences among the four serotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The exponential used to fit the distributions for DV1, DV2 and DV4 VLPs gives an effective rate constant for a first-order 'rate-limiting step'.
source: The exponential used to fit the distributions for DV1, DV2 and DV4 VLPs gives an effective rate constant for a first-order 'rate-limiting step'; the best formal fit for DV3 includes two successive or parallel steps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data fitting results.

claim: The best formal fit for DV3 includes two successive or parallel steps.
source: The exponential used to fit the distributions for DV1, DV2 and DV4 VLPs gives an effective rate constant for a first-order 'rate-limiting step'; the best formal fit for DV3 includes two successive or parallel steps.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data fitting results.

claim: The bulk fusion vs. pH curve for DV3 is less sharply sigmoidal than the others.
source: The bulk fusion vs. pH curve is also less sharply sigmoidal than are the others.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: The effective first-order rate of fusion for DV1 is slower than for DV2 and DV3.
source: Although the inflection pH measured in bulk is similar for DV1, DV2 and DV3, the effective first-order rate of fusion for DV1 is slower.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The compound 3-110-22 inhibits DV2 infection with IC90 of 0.7 μM.
source: The compound 3-110-22 (Figure 3) inhibits DV2 infection with IC90 of 0.7 μM (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2012.

claim: The IC50 for DV2 VLP fusion measured in bulk was 1-2 μM for compound 3-110-22.
source: The IC50 for DV2 VLP fusion, measured in bulk, was 1–2 μM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Presence of the inhibitor 3-110-22 has spread the dwell-time distribution and introduced a clear rise and fall.
source: Comparison of Figure 3B with the DV2 VLP panel in Figure 2B shows that presence of the inhibitor has spread the distribution and introduced a clear rise and fall, suggesting that the inhibitor has retarded a step other than the one that is effectively rate-limiting in its absence.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing experimental data in Figures 3B and 2B.

claim: The inhibitor 3-110-22 has retarded a step other than the one that is effectively rate-limiting in its absence.
source: Comparison of Figure 3B with the DV2 VLP panel in Figure 2B shows that presence of the inhibitor has spread the distribution and introduced a clear rise and fall, suggesting that the inhibitor has retarded a step other than the one that is effectively rate-limiting in its absence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the change in the dwell-time distribution shape.

claim: A fluorescent probe (Alexa-555) was conjugated to 3-110-22 at the 4-position of the benzene ring.
source: To relate single-particle hemifusion dwell-time distribution and small-molecule occupancy, we conjugated a fluorescent probe (Alexa-555) to 3-110-22 at the 4-position of the benzene ring (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: The IC50 of Alexa-555/3-110-22 is about 10- to 20-fold higher than that of the unmodified compound 3-110-22.
source: We confirmed that the modified form of the inhibitor was active by recording bulk hemifusion inhibition and found its IC50 to be about 10- to 20-fold higher that of the unmodified compound; the strong tendency of these hydrophobic compounds to associate in solution reduces the effective monomer concentration, and the actual difference may be smaller (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The strong tendency of these hydrophobic compounds to associate in solution reduces the effective monomer concentration.
source: We confirmed that the modified form of the inhibitor was active by recording bulk hemifusion inhibition and found its IC50 to be about 10- to 20-fold higher that of the unmodified compound; the strong tendency of these hydrophobic compounds to associate in solution reduces the effective monomer concentration, and the actual difference may be smaller (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed difference in IC50 values.

claim: 3-110-22 competed for binding with the modified inhibitor Alexa-555/3-110-22.
source: We also showed that 3-110-22 competed for binding with the modified inhibitor, indicating that they both interact at the same site (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 3-110-22 and Alexa-555/3-110-22 both interact at the same site.
source: We also showed that 3-110-22 competed for binding with the modified inhibitor, indicating that they both interact at the same site (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an inference from the competition binding data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At pH 5.5, the overall yield of hemifusion in the absence of inhibitor was approximately 25%.
source: At pH 5.5 under the conditions of our experiment, the overall yield of hemifusion in the absence of inhibitor was ~25% (i.e. the percent of total particles in the observation field that ultimately fused).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Particles with more than about 12 bound inhibitors failed to fuse at all.
source: Particles with more than about 12 bound inhibitors failed to fuse at all (Figure 4).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Particles with more than about 60 copies of Alexa-555/33-110-22 were not detected.
source: We did not detect particles with more than about 60 copies of Alexa-555/33-110-22, showing that binding saturated at an occupancy consistent with a large fraction of 'small VLPs' (~60 E subunits) in the preparation.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Binding saturated at an occupancy consistent with a large fraction of 'small VLPs' (~60 E subunits) in the preparation.
source: We did not detect particles with more than about 60 copies of Alexa-555/33-110-22, showing that binding saturated at an occupancy consistent with a large fraction of 'small VLPs' (~60 E subunits) in the preparation.
evidence: This is an inference from the saturation binding data.

claim: The contact zone between the particle and the membrane includes about 30 E subunits.
source: Assuming that the contact zone between the particle and the membrane includes about 30 E subunits (i.e. about half a small VLP) and that binding at one site is independent of the occupancy of any other site, then ~6 bound inhibitors in the contact should block fusion completely.
evidence: This is an assumption based on previous work.

claim: Approximately 6 bound inhibitors in the contact zone should block fusion completely, assuming independent binding.
source: Assuming that the contact zone between the particle and the membrane includes about 30 E subunits (i.e. about half a small VLP) and that binding at one site is independent of the occupancy of any other site, then ~6 bound inhibitors in the contact should block fusion completely.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the assumption of 30 E subunits in the contact zone and 12 inhibitors per particle blocking fusion.

claim: The percent of uncleaved prM was between 10 and 20% for various preparations.
source: The percent of uncleaved prM, estimated from Western blots, was between 10 and 20% for various preparations.
evidence: This is experimental data from Western blots.

claim: Residual uncleaved prM is usually found in a single cluster on virus particles.
source: Residual uncleaved prM is usually found in a single cluster on virus particles (Plevka et al., 2011); it should therefore be absent from the contact zone with the target membrane, to which the prM associated E cannot attach.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plevka et al., 2011.

claim: prM-associated E cannot attach to the contact zone with the target membrane.
source: Residual uncleaved prM is usually found in a single cluster on virus particles (Plevka et al., 2011); it should therefore be absent from the contact zone with the target membrane, to which the prM associated E cannot attach.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of prM-associated E.

claim: If there were no binding of the fluorescent inhibitor to prM-associated E, the estimate for the number of bound inhibitors per fully mature particle needed to prevent fusion completely would be about 14, rather than 12.
source: If there were no binding of the fluorescent inhibitor to prM-associated E, our estimate for the number of bound inhibitors per fully mature particle needed to prevent fusion completely would be about 14, rather than 12, or 7 in the contact zone, rather than 6.
evidence: This is a calculation adjusting for the presence of uncleaved prM.

claim: Presence of a small fraction of uncleaved prM on the particles would have had at most a relatively small effect on the determination of the inhibitory threshold.
source: Thus, presence of a small fraction of uncleaved prM on the particles in our experiments would have had at most a relatively small effect on our determination of the inhibitory threshold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculation of the adjusted inhibitor numbers.

claim: The conformational steps preceding hemifusion were modeled with a stochastic simulation.
source: We modeled the conformational steps preceding hemifusion with a stochastic simulation, structured like the scheme we used for simulations of West Nile virus hemifusion (Figure 2C) (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the computational method used, supported by citation.

claim: A hexagonal array of 30 E protomers represents the contact patch between viral and cell membranes in the simulation.
source: A hexagonal array of 30 E protomers represents the contact patch between viral and cell membranes.
evidence: This describes the simulation model structure.

claim: Each E subunit transits between an inactive state (in a dimer) and an activated monomer in the simulation.
source: Each E subunit transits between an inactive state (in a dimer) and an activated monomer, which can trimerize when two other adjacent monomers are activated.
evidence: This describes the simulation model structure.

claim: Hemifusion occurs upon formation of two adjacent trimers in the simulation.
source: Hemifusion occurs upon formation of two adjacent trimers.
evidence: This describes the simulation model structure.

claim: A cooperativity factor increases the probability of activation when the dimer partner is already activated in the simulation.
source: Dimer pairs are explicitly defined in the simulation, and a cooperativity factor increases the probability of activation when the dimer partner is already activated.
evidence: This describes the simulation model structure.

claim: The threshold for trimerization was set to pH 5.4 in the simulation.
source: The threshold for trimerization was set to pH 5.4, the bulk threshold for hemifusion, based on our previous finding that these two thresholds are the same for WNV (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes a simulation parameter based on previous findings.

claim: The trimerization threshold and bulk hemifusion threshold are the same for WNV.
source: The threshold for trimerization was set to pH 5.4, the bulk threshold for hemifusion, based on our previous finding that these two thresholds are the same for WNV (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chao et al., 2014.

claim: The assumption of reversibility for the DV2 E dimer-monomer transition comes from dynamic light scattering measurements performed on Kunjin virus.
source: The assumption of reversibility for the DV2 E dimer-monomer transition comes from dynamic light scattering measurements performed on Kunjin virus (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chao et al., 2014.

claim: The DV2 simulation produced a dwell time histogram at pH 5.5 that could be fit with a single exponential decay.
source: The DV2 simulation produced a dwell time histogram at pH 5.5 that could be fit with a single exponential decay (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In the simulation, the yield for particles achieving hemifusion was approximately 25%.
source: In our simulation, the yield for particles achieving hemifusion (defined as the total number of fusion events in a time window divided by the total number of identified particles) was ~25%, as observed experimentally.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation that matches experimental observations.

claim: The single-particle fusion kinetics for VLPs of all four dengue serotypes are qualitatively similar to those of WNV.
source: The single-particle fusion kinetics for VLPs of all four dengue serotypes are qualitatively similar to those of WNV (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of experimental data with previous work.

claim: Explicit simulation of DV2 fusion corresponds to direct experimental observation, for values of the simulation parameters close to those used to fit corresponding data for WNV.
source: Moreover, explicit simulation of DV2 fusion corresponds to direct experimental observation, for values of the simulation parameters close to those used to fit corresponding data for WNV.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of simulation and experimental results.

claim: The E proteins of WNV and the four serotypes of dengue virus are closely related to each other.
source: The E proteins of WNV and the four serotypes of dengue virus are closely related to each other, and their comparable in vitro fusion properties support the robustness of both our experimental design and our fusion model.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flavivirus E protein relationships.

claim: The comparable in vitro fusion properties of WNV and dengue E proteins support the robustness of both the experimental design and the fusion model.
source: The E proteins of WNV and the four serotypes of dengue virus are closely related to each other, and their comparable in vitro fusion properties support the robustness of both our experimental design and our fusion model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of fusion properties across related viruses.

claim: Inhibition of dengue virus fusion by 33-110-22 confirms its likely mode of action in blocking infection.
source: Inhibition of dengue virus fusion by 33-110-22, shown previously in bulk assays, confirms its likely mode of action in blocking infection (Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the fusion inhibition data and previous work.

claim: The inhibitor 3-110-22 and its analogs bind E on the virion surface before the particle attaches to a cell.
source: The inhibitor and its analogs bind E on the virion surface before the particle attaches to a cell, at a site on each of the E monomers that closes up during the transition from prefusion dimer to postfusion trimer (Modis et al., 2003, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2012; de Wispelaere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The inhibitor binds at a site on each of the E monomers that closes up during the transition from prefusion dimer to postfusion trimer.
source: The inhibitor and its analogs bind E on the virion surface before the particle attaches to a cell, at a site on each of the E monomers that closes up during the transition from prefusion dimer to postfusion trimer (Modis et al., 2003, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2012; de Wispelaere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The bound inhibitor molecules appear to fix the E protein in the conformation present in the prefusion dimer, blocking progression along the fusogenic pathway.
source: The bound molecules appear to fix the E protein in the conformation present in the prefusion dimer, blocking progression along the fusogenic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The cyanohydrazone inhibitors lock the hinge in a dimer-like configuration, even in the context of a fusion-intermediate trimer.
source: We have shown that the assay originally used to identify the cyanohydrzone inhibitors probably worked because these molecules lock the hinge in a dimer-like configuration, even in the context of a fusion-intermediate trimer (Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2013.

claim: Synthesis of a fluorescent derivative enabled determination of fusion efficiency as a function of the number of molecules bound.
source: Synthesis of a fluorescent derivative has now enabled us to examine its effects on a single-particle basis and hence to derive not only a bulk inhibitory IC50 but to determine the fusion efficiency as a function of the number of molecules bound.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and its advantages.

claim: Most of the particles in the preparations were small, ~60 subunit VLPs.
source: Most of the particles in our preparations were small, ~60 subunit VLPs.
evidence: This is an observation from the VLP preparations.

claim: About 6-7 inhibited monomers in a 30-monomer contact zone (a fractional occupancy of about 0.2) will be enough to prevent fusion completely.
source: The experimental results show that about 6–7 inhibited monomers in a 30-monomer contact zone (a fractional occupancy of about 0.2) will be enough to prevent fusion completely (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Virions, virion-sized (180-subunit) VLPs, and small VLPs have indistinguishable fusion kinetics, including their pH dependence.
source: Our previous work with WNV VLPs showed that virions, virion-sized (180-subunit) VLPs, and small VLPs have indistinguishable fusion kinetics, including their pH dependence (Chao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chao et al., 2014.

claim: About 35 inhibitors per dengue virion (about 20% occupancy) should block any detectable fusion.
source: Therefore, about 35 inhibitors per dengue virion (i.e. about 20% occupancy) should block any detectable fusion, assuming that for complete inhibition the threshold density of bound inhibitor is the same for the two size classes.
evidence: This is a calculation based on scaling from small VLPs to virions.

claim: Complete (or nearly complete) inhibition should occur at concentrations substantially lower than the Kd for an individual binding event.
source: An important inference is that complete (or nearly complete) inhibition should occur at concentrations substantially lower than the Kd for an individual binding event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that only 20% occupancy is needed for complete inhibition.

claim: Randomly inactivating seven monomers in the 30-monomer contact zone does not lead to full inhibition without further restrictions on the model.
source: In the simulation scheme in Figure 1B, modeling the effect of inhibitor binding to a monomer, at any step in the fusogenic conformational change, by inactivating at random seven monomers does not lead to full inhibition without further restrictions on the model.
evidence: This is a result from simulation analysis.

claim: There are ways of distributing inactivated monomers within the 30-monomer contact zone that still allow two neighboring, activated trimers to form, although in general more slowly than if all monomers could participate.
source: That is, there are ways of distributing inactivated monomers within the 30-monomer contact zone that still allow two neighboring, activated trimers to form, although in general more slowly than if all monomers could participate (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from simulation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: One potential explanation for complete inhibition is failure of an inhibitor-free trimer to associate with the target membrane, leading to an abortive fold-back with insertion of the fusion loops into the virion membrane instead.
source: We suggest two potential explanations: (i) failure of an inhibitor-free trimer to associate with the target membrane, leading to an abortive fold-back with insertion of the fusion loops into the virion membrane instead
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Another potential explanation for complete inhibition is dimer cooperativity, such that binding of inhibitor to one dimer partner inactivates (with some probability) the other.
source: (ii) dimer cooperativity, such that binding of inhibitor to one dimer partner inactivates (with some probability) the other, for example, by inhibiting dimer dissociation, thereby preventing the unliganded partner from forming an active trimer with other neighbors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: The abortive trimer mechanism is precisely analogous to the mechanism that accounts for a closely related observation in studies of influenza virus fusion.
source: The former mechanism would add a dead-end side reaction to the trimer zippering step in Figure 1. It is precisely analogous to the mechanism that accounts for a closely related observation in studies of influenza virus fusion (Ivanovic and Harrison, 2015; Otterstrom et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to influenza virus fusion studies.

claim: A total of eight or nine inactive monomers in the contact zone would be enough to rule out formation of two adjacent, active trimers.
source: Both inspection of diagrams such as the one in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and modified simulations with randomly inactivated monomers in the contact zone show that a total of eight or nine inactive monomers in the contact zone -- just one or two in addition to the seven with bound inhibitor -- would be enough to rule out formation of two adjacent, active trimers.
evidence: This is a result from simulation analysis and diagram inspection.

claim: The abortive trimer model would require only a low frequency of dead-end events, with minimal effect on fusion yield or kinetics in the inhibitor-free case.
source: Thus, the abortive trimer model would require only a low frequency of dead-end events, with minimal effect on fusion yield or kinetics in the inhibitor-free case (see also the similar conclusion for influenza fusion: Ivanovic and Harrison, 2015)
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results and comparison with influenza fusion.

claim: The dimer cooperativity model would require a relatively low probability for inactivation of the unliganded dimer partner.
source: and the dimer cooperativity model would require a relatively low probability for inactivation of the unliganded dimer partner (e.g. only partial inhibition of dimer dissocation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results.

claim: The geometrical idealizations inherent in the current simulation model do not allow distinction between the abortive trimer and dimer cooperativity mechanisms.
source: The geometrical idealizations inherent in the current simulation model do not allow us to distinguish between these alternatives.
evidence: This is a limitation of the current simulation model acknowledged by the authors.
